turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

Oh, man. I am holding so much space for you right now. 

Carrying a secret that heavy—leaving every single morning, sitting in a café for nine hours, and performing normal life while your world feels upended—must be absolute emotional exhaustion. 

I can completely understand how you got trapped in this routine. Between the sudden shock of the layoff, the pressure to keep things steady, and having your parents staying under your roof, pretending probably felt like the easiest way to protect everyone and buy yourself time. 

But you must be so, so tired. 

There's zero judgment here. You are in survival mode. But sitting alone with this all day has to be a lonely place to be. How are you holding up right now, just emotionally and physically?

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

That context makes the weight you're carrying make so much sense. In our families, a career isn't just a job—it's collective pride. When your dad boasts about your package to your chacha, he’s wearing your success like a badge. Feeling like you might strip that away from him, especially in a room full of 300 relatives looking for gossip, sounds terrifying. No wonder you can't sleep.

You are carrying the expectations of an entire extended family on your shoulders every single day from 9 to 6. 

That room in two weeks feels like a wall, but you don't have to figure out how to face all 300 people tonight. Right now, the most important thing is getting you out of this isolation. 

Have you thought about what might happen if you just told your wife first? Not about the wedding, not about your dad—just about *you*, and how exhausted you are sitting in that café?

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

It is not terrible at all. Please don't add guilt on top of everything else you're carrying. 

You are trying to protect yourself, protect your father's pride, and avoid being the main topic of conversation for 300 people who love to compare and judge. Wanting to dodge that bullet isn't terrible—it's a totally human self-preservation instinct. 

If making up a work excuse for that one night buys you mental peace and saves you from a panic attack, you do what you need to do to survive right now.

My only concern isn't the wedding, though. It's *you*, sitting in that café tomorrow morning at 9 AM. The wedding excuse might buy you a pass for that one night, but it won't take away the daily exhaustion of hiding this at home. 

How does your chest feel when you think about using that excuse? Does it feel like a relief, or just another layer of the secret?

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

I completely see why your brain goes there. On paper, it feels like the cleanest solution: you bridge the gap quietly, shield everyone from the stress, and reveal it only when there's a happy ending attached. It’s a very rational way to protect the people you love.

The reason it makes you feel sick, though, is because of what it does to *you*. 

It puts an incredible, relentless pressure on your job hunt. Every rejection or quiet recruiter suddenly isn't just about a job—it's about whether your secret holds up. That is an agonizing way to live for weeks or months, especially with the EMI clock ticking down in the background.

It makes complete sense why you're wavering between "this is fine" and sheer dread. 

If we take your father and the relatives out of the equation for a second... what is the scariest part about the idea of telling just your wife?
